title: Very good (Genesis 1:31)
hookLine: God made the world freely, out of goodness

lines: A GARDEN BED NOBODY ASKED FOR.
cards: A Saturday, and a neighbor is building a garden bed nobody asked for. No one is paying her. She doesn't even need the tomatoes; the store sells them.

Something in her is full and wants to spill over. When the last board is in, she steps back, wipes her hands, looks, and says one word: good. The Bible's first chapter ends with God stepping back and looking, too.

teach.b: First, the refrain. Genesis opens, in the Douay-Rheims: "In the beginning God created heaven, and earth." Day after day, as light, sea, plants and animals appear, the same line comes back: God saw that it was good.
And at the end, after human beings are made: "And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good." In Hebrew, tov me'od. Not just good.
The Catechism says God didn't create because he needed anything, but freely, out of wisdom and goodness, to share his own goodness.
Catholics say God was never alone, so creation isn't filling a gap; in their telling, it's love spilling over. Third, out of nothing.
Catholics believe God created from nothing at all, not from material lying around; in that view, everything exists because God wants it to, right now.

teach.h: GENESIS AND EVOLUTION: WHO, AND HOW.
teach.b: Then a quiet question: can I believe in evolution and still read Genesis as true? The Catechism says the six days are presented symbolically, a picture of God's work, not a stopwatch.
In 1950, Pope Pius the Twelfth left the development of the human body open to scientific study, while holding that each human soul is created directly by God.

In 1996, Pope John Paul the Second said new knowledge had led to recognizing evolution as more than a hypothesis. So a young-earth reading isn't Catholic teaching. Genesis tells who and why; science asks how.
The Catechism says each creature has its own particular goodness, reflecting something of God.
Saint Francis of Assisi sang to Brother Sun and Sister Moon, and Pope Francis took his 2015 letter on the environment, Laudato Si', from that song.
For Catholics, a world God called very good is worth noticing, thanking, and caring for.

how: Catholics profess God as creator of heaven and earth in the Creed at every Sunday Mass, bless animals on the feast of Saint Francis on October 4, and many now keep a Season of Creation each September.

games.q: God has finished making the world, including human beings. God steps back and looks. what's the verdict?
games.why: "And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good." only after humans appear does good become very good.

practice: Find something alive or natural near you, a plant on the sill, a tree through the window, a dog asleep, even your own breath, and look at it the way Genesis does: made on purpose, wanted into being. Say inside: very good.
If you pray, you can praise God for it, the way Francis did; if not, simply be glad it exists.

wordCard.voice: Creation. Everything God made freely, out of nothing, to share his goodness: and he called it very good. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: very good, God's verdict on everything at the end of the sixth day.

carryVoice: Your line: it was very good. It fits any living thing. That's day two hundred ninety-eight.
